summary.text: Isotopes are versions of the same chemical element that have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
Because they share an atomic number, they sit in the same place on the periodic table and have virtually the same chemical properties.
They differ in atomic mass and physical properties, and some are radioactive while others are stable.

facts.label: Name meaning
facts.value: Greek roots meaning the same place

facts.label: Term coined by
facts.value: Margaret Todd, in a 1913 suggestion to Frederick Soddy

facts.label: Carbon example
facts.value: Carbon-12, carbon-13 and carbon-14 have 6, 7 and 8 neutrons

facts.label: Soddy's prize
facts.value: The 1921 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, in part for isotopes

items.prompt: Two carbon atoms both have six protons, but one is heavier. What accounts for the difference?

options.label: More electrons packed into its nucleus
A different atomic number
More neutrons in its nucleus
A different chemical symbol

items.explain: Isotopes of an element share a proton count but have different numbers of neutrons, which gives them different mass numbers.

items.prompt: Two samples of the same element contain different isotopes. How will the samples compare?

options.label: Nearly identical chemistry, but different atomic masses
Completely different chemistry and the same mass
The same mass but different spots in the table
Different chemistry, since they have different atomic numbers

items.explain: All isotopes of a given element have virtually the same chemical properties, but different atomic masses and physical properties.

items.prompt: Chemists write carbon-14 for one form of carbon. What does the 14 count?

options.label: Protons only
Neutrons only
Electrons in the neutral atom
Protons and neutrons together

items.explain: The 14 is the mass number, the number of nucleons (protons and neutrons) in the nucleus, and carbon-14 has the mass number 14.

items.prompt: Several radioactive substances that looked like separate new elements could not be pulled apart by chemistry. What did Soddy propose?

options.label: Chemical separation just needs higher temperatures
Atoms with different radioactive properties can share one spot in the table
Radioactive substances cannot be true elements
Each substance needs its own box in the table

items.explain: Soddy proposed that several types of atoms, differing in radioactive properties, could occupy the same place in the table.

items.prompt: A sample of carbon holds atoms that, unlike their neighbours of the same element, give off radiation as they change. How do chemists classify them?

options.label: Stable isotopes of carbon
Atoms of a new element
Radioisotopes of carbon
Atoms with no neutrons

items.explain: Radioactive isotopes are called radioisotopes; for example, carbon-14 is a radioactive form of carbon, while carbon-12 and carbon-13 are stable.

items.prompt: An element has both stable and radioactive isotopes. Which kind will usually make up most of that element's atoms on Earth?

options.label: The radioactive ones, since they are newer
The stable ones, in most cases
An even split between the two kinds
Whichever isotope is the lightest

items.explain: In most cases, if an element has stable isotopes, those isotopes predominate in its abundance on Earth and in the Solar System.
